title: If Scripture's divinity is doubted, prove it a posteriori — not from faith principles
source_text: XIX. Sed quemadmodum, si prima cujusdam scientiae principia negentur ab homine contentioso, non probantur illa ex seipsis, sed illius scientiae fines transire necesse est, & aliunde eorum probationes quaerere: aut etiam recurrere ad quaedam minus nota quibus probentur a posteriori, & ad hominem illum; neque hoc quicquam derogat principiorum illorum perfectioni & sufficientiae: Ita si Scripturarum sacrarum divinitas in dubium vocetur, ut fit ab Ethnicis & profanis hominibus, probanda quidem erit, non tamen ex proprio earum testimonio, aut ex alio quopiam fidei principio, neque amplius suppetunt probationes quas vocant de fide, hoc est, quae petitae sint ex proprie dictis fidei principiis: sed aliae probationes adhibendae erunt, quae petentur ex variis notis, tum intus, tum externis, quibus Scripturae Sacrae divinitas innotescere, & confirmari potest. Neque hoc obstat quominus, fidelium respectu, plenissima sit & perfectissima religionis & fidei regula.
pass_a_gloss: But just as, if the first principles of some science are denied by a contentious man, they are not proved from themselves, but it is necessary to cross the bounds of that science and seek their proofs from elsewhere: or even to recur to certain things less known by which they are proved a posteriori, and to that man; and this does not at all derogate from the perfection and sufficiency of those principles: So if the divinity of the sacred Scriptures is called into doubt, as happens by Gentiles and profane men, it will indeed have to be proved, yet not from their own proper testimony, or from any other principle of faith, nor are there any longer available the proofs they call of faith, that is, which are sought from principles of faith properly so called: but other proofs will have to be employed, which will be sought from various marks, both inward and external, by which the divinity of Sacred Scripture can become known and be confirmed. Nor does this hinder that, with respect to believers, it is the fullest and most perfect rule of religion and faith.
pass_b_english: If a contentious man denies a science's first principles, you do not prove them from themselves. You must leave that science's bounds and seek proofs elsewhere — or even use weaker, a posteriori arguments aimed at that man. That does not lessen the principles' perfection or sufficiency.

So if Gentiles and profane men call Scripture's divinity into doubt, it must be proved — yet not from Scripture's own testimony, nor from any other faith principle. The proofs called de fide (drawn from faith principles properly so named) no longer apply.

Other proofs must be used: various marks, inward and outward, by which Scripture's divinity can be known and confirmed. That still leaves Scripture, for believers, the fullest and most perfect rule of religion and faith.
